question: Read $\Box$ as "the agent knows that". Which closure condition, on its own, commits the agent to knowing every theorem of logic?
options: Distribution, since it closes knowledge under implication
Necessitation, since it makes every theorem of logic boxed
The conjunction principle, since it lets known items be combined
Replacement of provable equivalents, since every theorem is equivalent to every other
explanation: Necessitation takes any theorem $\varphi$ to $\Box \varphi$ directly, which is the logical omniscience problem the article says epistemic logic avoids by dropping it. Distribution only closes knowledge under implication: it spreads what is already known but needs something known to start from.

question: Lewis introduced strict implication to escape the paradoxes of material implication. Which analogous paradox does strict implication itself face?
options: Any false sentence strictly implies every sentence whatever
Any true sentence is strictly implied by every sentence whatever
Strict implication is not transitive
Any necessary truth is strictly implied by every sentence
explanation: If $\psi$ is necessary, no world makes $\varphi$ true and $\psi$ false, so $\varphi$ strictly implies $\psi$ whatever $\varphi$ says. The options about merely false or merely true sentences describe the original material paradoxes, which strict implication does avoid, because a contingent truth can fail at some other world.

question: A relational model is the special case of a neighbourhood model in which the neighbourhoods of a world are which sets?
options: Exactly the supersets of the set of worlds it accesses
Exactly the subsets of the set of worlds it accesses
Exactly the singletons of the worlds it accesses
Exactly the set of worlds it accesses, and nothing else
explanation: Relationally, $\Box \varphi$ holds at $w$ when every accessible world satisfies $\varphi$, that is, when the truth set of $\varphi$ contains the accessible set; so the neighbourhoods must be its supersets. Taking only the accessible set itself would make $\Box \varphi$ true only when $\varphi$ holds at exactly the accessible worlds, which is far too demanding.

question: Worlds $w$, $u$, $v$. The sentence $p$ is true at $u$ only, $q$ at $v$ only, and the neighbourhoods of $w$ are exactly $\{u\}$ and $\{v\}$. Which of these fails at $w$?
options: $\Box(p \land q) \rightarrow \Box p$
$\Box p \rightarrow \Box \neg\neg p$
$(\Box p \land \Box q) \rightarrow \Box(p \land q)$
$\Box q \rightarrow \Box(q \land q)$
explanation: The truth sets of $p$ and $q$ are both neighbourhoods, but that of $p \land q$ is empty and is not, so the conjunction principle fails: the neighbourhoods are not closed under intersection. The monotonicity instance survives only because its antecedent $\Box(p \land q)$ is false here, and the other two replace a sentence by one with the same truth set.

question: In a neighbourhood model every world's neighbourhoods are closed under supersets and under intersection, but some world has no neighbourhoods at all. Which principle of the normal systems fails?
options: Distribution, since closure under supersets is weaker than an accessibility relation
Necessitation, since $\Box \top$ is false at that world
The conjunction principle, having nothing to intersect
Replacement of provable equivalents, since that world gives $\Box$ no truth sets at all
explanation: Necessitation corresponds to containing the set of all worlds, and an empty collection does not, so $\Box \top$ fails there. Monotonicity and the conjunction principle together already yield distribution, which is why the tempting first option is wrong: the only thing missing is the unit.

question: In a neighbourhood model with no closure conditions at all, if $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are true at exactly the same worlds, then $\Box \varphi$ and $\Box \psi$ are true at exactly the same worlds.
options: True
False
explanation: Whether $\Box \varphi$ holds depends only on whether the truth set of $\varphi$ is a neighbourhood, so sentences with the same truth set get the same verdict. That is why even the weakest system E keeps replacement of equivalents; dropping closure conditions does not by itself separate necessarily equivalent sentences, which is the job impossible worlds take on.

question: Why does deontic logic want the conjunction principle to fail?
options: It would make every theorem of logic obligatory, however trivial the theorem
Obligations are not closed under logical equivalence, so a conjunction of them can differ from its parts
Conflicting obligations cannot both be true at one world, so the principle would never apply to them
Obligations to do $\varphi$ and to do $\neg \varphi$ would yield an obligation to do everything
explanation: With the conjunction principle the two obligations yield $\Box(\varphi \land \neg \varphi)$, and monotonicity then delivers an obligation to do anything at all. Making every theorem obligatory is the effect of necessitation, a different principle with a different deontic complaint.

question: In Kripke's semantics for S2 and S3, normal world $w$ accesses only $n$, a non-normal world. Which of these is false at $w$?
options: $p \lor \neg p$
$\Box(p \lor \neg p)$
$\Box\Box(p \lor \neg p)$
$\Diamond(p \lor \neg p)$
explanation:
A non-normal world still evaluates the connectives classically, so $p \lor 
eg p$ is true at $n$ and $\Box(p \lor 
eg p)$ holds at $w$. What fails at $n$ is every boxed sentence, so $\Box(p \lor 
eg p)$ is false there and its necessitation is false at $w$; the trap is thinking non-normal worlds falsify everything.

question: If a proposition is a set of possible worlds, why does believing one mathematical truth amount to believing all of them?
options: Belief is closed under logical consequence, and mathematical truths all follow from one another
Every mathematical truth holds at every possible world, so all are one proposition
Necessitation makes every mathematical truth believed by any agent who believes one of them
Mathematical truths share one content, being provable from the same axioms
explanation: Two necessary truths are true at exactly the same possible worlds, so on this account there is only one necessary proposition to believe. The closure option describes a different failing (logical omniscience) that does not depend on how propositions are individuated; impossible worlds address the individuation problem by letting the truths come apart somewhere.

question: The objection says the weak systems are "model theory for propositional attitudes wearing the notation of logic". What is the core of the reply?
options: Modal logic is unified by a question, which principles govern an operator on propositions
Belief and obligation are, on analysis, species of metaphysical necessity, so the notation fits them
The weak systems validate necessitation once impossible worlds are added
Non-normal systems came after Kripke semantics and so inherit its standing as a logic of necessity
explanation: The reply denies that the box was ever fixed as metaphysical necessity: Lewis's systems concerned implication and deontic logic predates relational semantics. The historical option gets the order backwards, since the Lewis systems came first and Kripke semantics thirty years later.
